questions.q: In how many different ways can 5 different books be arranged on a shelf?
questions.e: Arranging 5 distinct items gives 5! = 5×4×3×2×1 = 120. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: How many different 3-digit codes can be made from the digits 1 to 5 if no digit is repeated?
questions.e: Order matters, so use P(5,3) = 5×4×3 = 60. (125 would allow repeats.) Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: How many ways can a president, a vice-president and a secretary be chosen from 8 people?
questions.e: The offices are different, so order matters: P(8,3) = 8×7×6 = 336. (56 is C(8,3), where order is ignored.) Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: How many committees of 4 can be chosen from 10 people?
questions.e: Order does not matter, so C(10,4) = (10×9×8×7)/4! = 210. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: In a group of 6 people, each person shakes hands with every other person exactly once. How many handshakes occur?
questions.e: Each handshake is a pair of people, so C(6,2) = 6×5/2 = 15. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: How many different 5-digit PIN codes can be made from the digits 0 to 9 if digits may be repeated?
questions.e: Each of the 5 positions has 10 choices, so 10⁵ = 100000. (30240 is the count without repeats.) Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: A shop sells 4 shirts, 3 trousers and 2 hats. How many different outfits (one of each) are possible?
questions.e: By the multiplication principle, 4 × 3 × 2 = 24. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: What is the value of 0! (zero factorial)?
questions.e: By definition 0! = 1, which keeps the formula C(n,0) = n!/(0!·n!) = 1 consistent. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: How many distinct arrangements of the letters of the word BANANA are there?
questions.e: 6!/(3!·2!) = 720/12 = 60, dividing by the repeats of A (3 times) and N (2 times). Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: How many distinct arrangements of the letters of the word LEVEL are there?
questions.e: 5!/(2!·2!) = 120/4 = 30, since L and E each appear twice. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: In how many ways can 5 people sit in a row if two particular people must sit next to each other?
questions.e: Treat the pair as one block: 4! arrangements of 4 units, times 2! orders inside the block = 24 × 2 = 48. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: In how many ways can 5 people be seated around a circular table (rotations count as the same)?
questions.e: Fix one person's seat to remove rotations; the other 4 can be arranged in 4! = 24 ways. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: A committee of 3 is chosen from 5 men and 4 women. How many committees contain exactly 2 women?
questions.e: Choose 2 of 4 women and 1 of 5 men: C(4,2) × C(5,1) = 6 × 5 = 30. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: How many subsets (including the empty set) does a set with 5 elements have?
questions.e: Each element is either in or out of a subset, giving 2⁵ = 32. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: A number plate has 2 letters (26 choices each) followed by 3 digits (10 choices each), repeats allowed. How many plates are possible?
questions.e: 26 × 26 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 676 000. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: In how many ways can 2 cards be dealt from a 52-card deck if the order of the cards does not matter?
questions.e: C(52,2) = (52×51)/2 = 1326. (2652 counts ordered pairs.) Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: How many diagonals does a regular hexagon have?
questions.e: Any two of the 6 vertices make a segment: C(6,2) = 15. Remove the 6 sides to leave 9 diagonals. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: How many even 3-digit numbers can be formed from the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 without repeating a digit?
questions.e: The last digit must be 2 or 4 (2 choices); the first two digits can then be chosen in 4 × 3 ways: 2 × 12 = 24. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Choosing a team of 3 players from 10, where the order of selection does not matter, is an example of:
questions.e: When order is irrelevant, the count is a combination, C(10,3). Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Which formula gives the number of combinations C(n, r)?
questions.e: C(n,r) = n!/(r!(n − r)!). The formula n!/(n − r)! is P(n,r), which counts ordered selections. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: A fair coin is tossed 3 times. What is the probability of getting 3 heads?
questions.e: There are 2³ = 8 equally likely outcomes and only HHH qualifies, so 1/8. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: A fair coin is tossed 3 times. What is the probability of getting exactly 2 heads?
questions.e: The favourable outcomes are HHT, HTH and THH: 3 out of 8, so 3/8. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: A fair coin is tossed 3 times. What is the probability of getting at least one head?
questions.e: Use the complement: 1 − P(no heads) = 1 − 1/8 = 7/8. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Two fair coins are tossed. What is the probability of getting exactly one head?
questions.e: The outcomes HH, HT, TH, TT are equally likely; HT and TH give one head, so 2/4 = 1/2. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: A fair die is rolled once. What is the probability of getting a prime number?
questions.e: The primes on a die are 2, 3 and 5 (1 is not prime), so 3/6 = 1/2. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: A fair die is rolled once. What is the probability of getting an even number or a number greater than 4?
questions.e: The favourable numbers are 2, 4, 5, 6 (6 is counted once): 4/6 = 2/3. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is 7?
questions.e: The pairs (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1) give 6 of the 36 outcomes, so 1/6. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the product of the two numbers is even?
questions.e: The product is odd only when both numbers are odd: 3/6 × 3/6 = 1/4. So P(even) = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: One card is drawn at random from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability that it is an ace?
questions.e: There are 4 aces among 52 cards: 4/52 = 1/13. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: One card is drawn from a standard deck. What is the probability that it is a heart or a king?
questions.e: 13 hearts + 4 kings − 1 king of hearts (counted twice) = 16 cards, so 16/52 = 4/13. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: One card is drawn from a standard deck. What is the probability that it is a red face card (J, Q or K)?
questions.e: There are 3 face cards in each of the 2 red suits: 6/52 = 3/26. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: A bag holds 5 red, 3 blue and 2 green balls. Two balls are drawn together. What is the probability that both are red?
questions.e: C(5,2)/C(10,2) = 10/45 = 2/9. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Which of these numbers cannot be the probability of an event?
questions.e: Probabilities must lie between 0 and 1 inclusive, so 1.2 is impossible. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: If P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A and B) = 0.2, what is P(A or B)?
questions.e: Addition rule: P(A or B) = 0.4 + 0.5 − 0.2 = 0.7. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: A and B are mutually exclusive events with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.45. What is P(A or B)?
questions.e: Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together, so the probabilities simply add: 0.3 + 0.45 = 0.75. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Two coins and one die are tossed together. How many outcomes are in the sample space?
questions.e: By the multiplication principle: 2 × 2 × 6 = 24. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: A two-digit number from 10 to 99 is chosen at random. What is the probability that it is divisible by 5?
questions.e: The multiples of 5 from 10 to 95 number 18 out of 90 two-digit numbers: 18/90 = 1/5. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: A letter is chosen at random from the word MATHEMATICS. What is the probability that it is a vowel?
questions.e: The word has 11 letters, of which A, E, A, I are vowels (4), so 4/11. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: A fair die is rolled 3 times. What is the probability of getting at least one six?
questions.e: Use the complement: 1 − (5/6)³ = 1 − 125/216 = 91/216. (Adding 3 × 1/6 = 1/2 is wrong because the events overlap.) Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: The probabilities of all the outcomes in a sample space add up to:
questions.e: Exactly one outcome must occur, so the probabilities of all possible outcomes total 1. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Two fair dice are rolled. Given that the first die shows 3, what is the probability that the sum is 8?
questions.e: With the first die fixed at 3, the second must be 5: probability 1/6. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Two fair dice are rolled. Given that at least one die shows 5, what is the probability that the sum is 10?
questions.e: 11 of the 36 outcomes contain a 5; only (5,5) has sum 10. So 1/11. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: A fair die is rolled and the result is known to be even. What is the probability it is greater than 3?
questions.e: The reduced sample space is {2, 4, 6}; two of these (4 and 6) exceed 3, so 2/3. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: If P(A and B) = 0.12 and P(B) = 0.4, what is P(A given B)?
questions.e: P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B) = 0.12/0.4 = 0.3. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: In a class, 60% of students pass Maths and 40% of all students pass both Maths and Physics. What fraction of Maths passers also pass Physics?
questions.e: P(Physics | Maths) = 0.40/0.60 = 2/3. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: In a class of 40, 25 like cricket, 15 like football and 5 like both. A student who likes cricket is chosen. What is the probability they also like football?
questions.e: Restrict to the 25 cricket fans; 5 of them like football, so 5/25 = 1/5. (5/15 would be the other way round.) Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Three fair coins are tossed and the first one is a head. What is the probability that there are exactly 2 heads in total?
questions.e: Given the first head, the other two coins must show exactly one head: 2 of 4 equally likely cases, so 1/2. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: If P(A) = 0.5 and P(B given A) = 0.4, what is P(A and B)?
questions.e: Multiplication rule: P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B|A) = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: A and B are independent events with P(A) = 0.5 and P(B) = 0.2. What is P(A and B)?
questions.e: For independent events P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B) = 0.5 × 0.2 = 0.1. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: A and B are independent events with P(A) = 0.6 and P(B) = 0.5. What is P(A or B)?
questions.e: P(neither) = 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.2, so P(A or B) = 1 − 0.2 = 0.8. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: A fair coin has just landed heads four times in a row. What is the probability that the next toss is a head?
questions.e: Tosses are independent, so past results do not change the next toss: the probability stays 1/2. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Two cards are drawn without replacement from a standard deck. What is the probability that both are aces?
questions.e: 4/52 × 3/51 = 12/2652 = 1/221. (1/169 would be drawing with replacement.) Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Two cards are drawn without replacement from a standard deck. Given that the first is a king, what is the probability that the second is also a king?
questions.e: After removing one king, 3 kings remain among 51 cards: 3/51 = 1/17. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Two cards are drawn without replacement from a standard deck. What is the probability that both are red?
questions.e: 26/52 × 25/51 = 650/2652 = 25/102. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: A bag has 4 red and 6 blue balls. Two are drawn one after the other without replacement. What is the probability that both are blue?
questions.e: 6/10 × 5/9 = 30/90 = 1/3. (9/25 would be drawing with replacement.) Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: A bag has 3 red and 2 black balls. Two balls are drawn one at a time, replacing the first before the second. What is the probability that both are red?
questions.e: With replacement the draws are independent: 3/5 × 3/5 = 9/25. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Machine A makes 60% of a factory's items and machine B makes 40%. 2% of A's items and 5% of B's are defective. What is the probability that a randomly chosen item is defective?
questions.e: Total probability: 0.6 × 0.02 + 0.4 × 0.05 = 0.012 + 0.020 = 0.032. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Machine A makes 60% of items (2% defective) and machine B makes 40% (5% defective). A defective item is found. What is the probability it came from machine A?
questions.e: Bayes' rule: P(A | defective) = 0.012/0.032 = 0.375. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Events A and B both have positive probability and are mutually exclusive. Which statement is correct?
o: A and B are always independent
A and B are not independent
A and B must be complements of each other
A and B are independent only if P(A) = P(B)
questions.e: Mutually exclusive means P(A and B) = 0, but P(A)·P(B) > 0, so the product rule for independence fails. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Two events A and B are independent exactly when:
questions.e: Independence means knowing one event does not change the probability of the other, which is the product rule. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Find the mean of the data set 4, 8, 6, 10, 12.
questions.e: Sum = 40 and there are 5 values, so the mean is 40/5 = 8. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Find the median of the data set 12, 3, 7, 20, 5.
questions.e: Sorted: 3, 5, 7, 12, 20. The middle value is 7. (9.4 is the mean, not the median.) Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Find the median of 2, 4, 6, 10, 12, 20.
questions.e: With 6 values, average the two middle ones: (6 + 10)/2 = 8. (The mean is 9.) Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: What is the mode of the data set 2, 2, 3, 5, 5, 7?
questions.e: Both 2 and 5 appear twice, which is the highest frequency, so the data set is bimodal. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Find the range of the data 4, 9, 15, 2, 11.
questions.e: Range = largest − smallest = 15 − 2 = 13. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Find the population variance of 1, 3, 5, 7, 9.
questions.e: The mean is 5, the squared deviations are 16, 4, 0, 4, 16 (sum 40), and 40/5 = 8. (Dividing by 4 would give the sample variance, 10.) Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Find the sample variance of 2, 4, 6 (divide by n − 1).
questions.e: The mean is 4, the squared deviations are 4, 0, 4 (sum 8), and 8/(3 − 1) = 4. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Find the population standard deviation of 3, 3, 7, 7.
questions.e: The mean is 5, every deviation is ±2, so the variance is 4 and the standard deviation is √4 = 2. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Every value in a data set is increased by 10. What happens to the standard deviation?
questions.e: Adding a constant shifts all values equally, so the distances between them (the spread) do not change. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Every value in a data set is multiplied by 3. If the original standard deviation was 4, what is the new standard deviation?
questions.e: Multiplying every value by 3 multiplies the standard deviation by 3: 3 × 4 = 12. (The variance would be multiplied by 9.) Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Which measure of centre is least affected by one extremely large outlier?
questions.e: The median depends only on the middle position, while the mean, range and variance all change a lot when one value is extreme. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: In a test, 3 students scored 60, 2 scored 80 and 5 scored 70. What is the mean score?
questions.e: Weighted sum = 180 + 160 + 350 = 690, divided by 10 students gives 69. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: The mean of 5 numbers is 12. A sixth number is added and the mean becomes 14. What is the sixth number?
questions.e: The new total is 14 × 6 = 84 and the old total was 12 × 5 = 60, so the new number is 24. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: The mean of the numbers 3, 7, x, 10 and 5 is 7. What is x?
questions.e: The total must be 7 × 5 = 35, so x = 35 − (3 + 7 + 10 + 5) = 10. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: A frequency table shows the value 1 occurring 2 times, 2 occurring 5 times and 3 occurring 3 times. What is the mean value?
questions.e: Sum = 1×2 + 2×5 + 3×3 = 21 over 10 observations, so the mean is 2.1. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Class A has 20 students with mean mark 60. Class B has 30 students with mean mark 70. What is the combined mean?
questions.e: Combined total = 1200 + 2100 = 3300 over 50 students = 66. (The simple average 65 ignores class sizes.) Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: A student scores 70 in a test where the mean is 60 and the standard deviation is 5. What is the z-score?
questions.e: z = (x − mean)/SD = (70 − 60)/5 = 2. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: In a right-skewed distribution (a long tail of large values), which is usually true?
o: The mean is less than the median
The mean is greater than the median
The mode is always the largest value
questions.e: Large values in the right tail pull the mean upwards, while the median is hardly affected. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Which of these can never be negative?
questions.e: The standard deviation is the square root of an average of squares, so it is zero or positive. A mean or median can be negative if the data are. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: The sample variance is calculated by dividing the sum of squared deviations by:
questions.e: Dividing by n − 1 (Bessel's correction) compensates for estimating the mean from the same sample. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: A fair coin is tossed 4 times. What is the probability of exactly 2 heads?
questions.e: Binomial: C(4,2)·(1/2)⁴ = 6/16 = 3/8. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: A fair die is rolled 3 times. What is the probability of exactly one six?
questions.e: Binomial: C(3,1)·(1/6)(5/6)² = 3 × 25/216 = 25/72. (Forgetting the factor 3 gives 25/216.) Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Each of 4 independent trials succeeds with probability 1/3. What is the probability of no successes at all?
questions.e: All four trials must fail: (2/3)⁴ = 16/81. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Each of 3 independent trials succeeds with probability 0.1. What is the probability of at least one success?
questions.e: Use the complement: 1 − 0.9³ = 1 − 0.729 = 0.271. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: A binomial random variable has n = 20 trials and success probability p = 0.25. What is its mean?
questions.e: The mean of a binomial distribution is np = 20 × 0.25 = 5. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: For a binomial distribution with n = 10 and p = 0.3, what is the variance np(1 − p)?
questions.e: Variance = np(1 − p) = 10 × 0.3 × 0.7 = 2.1. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: What is the expected value of the number shown on a fair six-sided die?
questions.e: E(X) = (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6)/6 = 21/6 = 3.5. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: In a game you win Rs 100 with probability 0.2 and lose Rs 20 otherwise. What is your expected gain per play?
questions.e: E = 100 × 0.2 + (−20) × 0.8 = 20 − 16 = Rs 4. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: A raffle sells 1000 tickets at Rs 10 each. There is one prize of Rs 5000. What is the expected net gain per ticket?
questions.e: The expected prize per ticket is 5000/1000 = Rs 5, and the ticket costs Rs 10, so the expected net is −Rs 5. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: A random variable X has P(X = 1) = 0.2, P(X = 2) = 0.5 and P(X = 3) = 0.3. What is E(X)?
questions.e: E(X) = 1(0.2) + 2(0.5) + 3(0.3) = 0.2 + 1.0 + 0.9 = 2.1. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: X takes values 0, 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 0.1, 0.4, k and 0.2. What is k?
questions.e: The probabilities must add to 1, so k = 1 − (0.1 + 0.4 + 0.2) = 0.3. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: If E(X²) = 10 and E(X) = 3, what is Var(X)?
questions.e: Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]² = 10 − 9 = 1. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: What is the variance of the number shown on one roll of a fair die?
questions.e: E(X²) = 91/6 and E(X) = 7/2, so Var = 91/6 − 49/4 = 35/12 (about 2.92). Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: A fair coin is tossed repeatedly until the first head appears. On average, how many tosses does this take?
questions.e: The expected number of trials until the first success is 1/p = 1/(1/2) = 2. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: If E(X) = 5, what is E(2X + 3)?
questions.e: Expectation is linear: E(2X + 3) = 2E(X) + 3 = 13. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: If Var(X) = 3, what is Var(3X + 1)?
questions.e: Adding a constant does not change variance, and multiplying by 3 multiplies it by 9: 9 × 3 = 27. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: X is uniformly distributed on the interval from 0 to 10. What is P(X > 7)?
questions.e: The probability is the length of the interval (7, 10) divided by the total length 10: 3/10 = 0.3. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Approximately what percentage of a normal distribution lies within 2 standard deviations of the mean?
questions.e: The empirical rule: about 68% within 1 SD, 95% within 2 SD and 99.7% within 3 SD. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Which situation is best modelled by a binomial distribution?
o: The number of heads in 10 tosses of a fair coin
The number of cards drawn without replacement until the first ace
The heights of 10 randomly chosen adults
The waiting time until a bus arrives
questions.e: A binomial count needs a fixed number of independent trials, each with the same success probability. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).

questions.q: Which list of values can be a probability distribution for a random variable with 3 outcomes?
questions.e: Each probability must be between 0 and 1 and the total must be exactly 1. Only 0.1 + 0.4 + 0.5 does this. Practice question written by Claude; topic outline follows OpenStax (CC BY 4.0).
